opus-5.5.text:
I think the key shift is that we're moving from scaling tokens in pretraining to scaling the tokens a model can use while it's actually working on a problem. For a long time, the main lever was more data and more compute during training, which gave models broad knowledge and good intuition. But knowledge alone doesn't get you through a complex task. Real tasks, like writing and debugging a large codebase, doing a research survey, or running a multi-step analysis, need the model to plan, try things, observe the results, notice mistakes, and revise. All of that consumes tokens. So the question becomes whether the model can use a very long trajectory productively, or whether it gets lost or degrades halfway through.

There are a few pieces that have to come together. The first is long context: if the model can't hold the history of what it has done, it can't reason over it. We made this a priority early on because we believed long context is the foundation for everything that comes after. The second is reasoning through reinforcement learning. When you train the model on outcomes rather than just imitating human text, it learns to think longer when the problem is harder. You start to see behaviors like reflection and backtracking emerge without explicitly programming them. The third is tool use and interaction with an environment. Once the model can search, execute code, and read the results, the tokens it generates aren't just internal monologue. They're actions with feedback, and that's where autonomy actually comes from.

What's exciting is that these dimensions compound. A model that can reason over a longer horizon can make better use of tools, and tool feedback gives it better signal to keep reasoning. In the past, a task might take a few hundred tokens of answer. Now we're talking about agents that run hundreds of steps and millions of tokens, and the quality of the final result keeps improving as you allow more of that. It's a new scaling curve.

Of course, there are real challenges. Errors accumulate over long trajectories, so stability and self-correction matter enormously. Efficiency matters too, because if every token is expensive you can't afford to let the model explore. And evaluation gets much harder when the task is open-ended. But I think the direction is clear. The ceiling of what AI can do autonomously is increasingly determined by how many tokens it can use effectively, not just how big the model is. For us, the goal is to push that frontier, so the model goes from being something that answers questions to something you can hand a real piece of work and trust it to finish.

r001.rationale: The response says complex tasks can use hundreds of steps and millions of tokens, but it does not state that scaling token use can increase the time those tasks take to finish.

fable-5.1.text:
I think token scaling is really the key variable behind what we now call agentic AI, and the way I'd frame it is this: the number of tokens a model can consume and produce in a single task is essentially a measure of how much "thinking" and "acting" it can do before it has to stop.

Early on, we were in a world where a model answered one question with a few hundred tokens. That's a conversation. But a complex task, say writing and debugging a piece of software, doing a research literature review, or planning a multi-step project, isn't a single answer. It's a long sequence of thinking, trying something, observing the result, revising, and trying again. Each of those steps costs tokens. So if you only have the budget for a few thousand tokens, you can only do very short tasks. If the model can reliably use hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens on one problem, suddenly the horizon of what it can finish on its own extends from minutes to hours or even days of human-equivalent work.

There are really three dimensions here. One is context length, how much the model can hold in working memory. Two is the amount of reasoning tokens, how long the model can "think" before it commits to an action, which is what reinforcement learning on long chains of thought has unlocked. And three is interaction tokens, the model calling tools, reading outputs, searching, running code, and feeding all of that back in. Agentic behavior comes from scaling all three together.

But I'd add that more tokens alone isn't enough. The model has to use them well. If you just let it think longer without training, it tends to drift, repeat itself, or lose track of the goal. So the real breakthrough is using RL to teach the model to allocate its token budget: when to explore, when to verify, when to back off and try another approach. Once the model learns that, you get a very nice scaling curve where more test-time compute reliably translates into higher success rates on harder tasks.

At Moonshot that's exactly the bet we've made with Kimi. We care less about how clever one answer looks and more about whether the model can sustain coherent, goal-directed work over a very long trajectory. In my view, that's where the next big jump in practical value comes from. The models don't necessarily have to get much smarter per token; they have to be able to spend far more tokens productively on a single problem. That's what makes it possible to hand over an entire task and come back later to a finished result.

r001.rationale: The response says that larger token budgets extend autonomous task horizons from minutes to hours or days, directly conveying that token scaling can support longer, more complex tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think token scaling gives us a way to move from answering a question to carrying out a whole task. A complex task usually requires many steps: you need to understand the goal, make a plan, try something, inspect the result, and revise your approach. If the model can use more tokens productively, it can spend more computation on that process instead of having to produce an answer immediately.

But more tokens alone are not enough. The model needs to learn how to use them—when to explore, when to verify, and when to stop. Otherwise, it can generate a longer chain of reasoning without making real progress. And for autonomous tasks, small mistakes can accumulate, so recognizing and recovering from errors becomes very important.

The exciting possibility is that we can allocate computation according to the difficulty of the task. A simple question might need very little. A complex project might require many rounds of reasoning, tool use, and feedback. If we can make that extended process reliable, then we can delegate increasingly substantial tasks to AI, rather than supervise every individual step.

r001.rationale: The response says more tokens can mean more computation and more rounds of reasoning, tool use, and feedback, but it does not clearly state that this increases the time needed to finish the task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think token scaling gives us a way to turn more computation into better problem solving at inference time. Instead of answering immediately, a model can spend more tokens breaking down a problem, exploring different approaches, checking intermediate results, and correcting mistakes.

For complex tasks, that matters because the answer is usually a sequence of actions. You need to make a plan, execute part of it, observe what happened, and update the plan. A coding task, for example, might require understanding a repository, making changes, running tests, and debugging failures. The system needs enough room to carry that process through.

But more tokens alone don’t guarantee autonomy. The model has to learn to use that budget effectively, recognize when an approach is failing, and verify whether it has actually achieved the goal. Otherwise, you can get a longer trajectory without a better result.

So the opportunity is to combine token scaling with training that rewards successful completion of longer tasks. If we can make additional computation reliably improve success rates, then we can gradually give systems more difficult tasks and longer periods of independent work.

r001.rationale: The response says more tokens let a model carry out a longer problem-solving process and that systems can take on tasks for “longer periods of independent work,” communicating that complex autonomous tasks can take more time to complete.
